channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Colorado confirms foreign actors got into two small drinking-water systems and changed how they ran — settings altered, alarms and remote access switched off, pumping cycles changed
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Governor Jared Polis’s office confirmed on 18 September that foreign actors breached two small, privately owned drinking-water providers in Colorado in late August. Neither provider has been named; each serves fewer than 200 people. According to the Governor’s office, the intruders changed equipment settings, disabled alarms and remote access, and altered pumping cycles. The state says the disruptions were brief, the providers corrected them and notified the state, and there was no known impact on water treatment, water quality or public safety. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) confirmed the problems were resolved and offered technical assistance, and the state has alerted other water providers to review their security measures and apply updates. Attribution is not confirmed and the intrusions should be read as the work of unattributed foreign actors. A spokesperson for the Governor’s office told Reuters the state “cannot confirm what foreign actors may have been involved, but we are aware of ongoing efforts across the nation by an Iranian-backed group to access drinking water and wastewater systems”; AP’s account ties that awareness to CISA. According to Reuters, CISA and the FBI declined to comment or did not respond, and no Colorado-specific federal advisory has been published. Denver Water, which serves about 1.5 million people, told Axios its systems were evaluated and are unaffected. AP reports the state is distributing new cybersecurity guidance to agencies. SecurityWeek’s 21 September account, citing the Denver Post, and Industrial Cyber’s 22 September write-up add no new facts beyond the Governor’s statement, and as of 24 September no further Colorado systems have been disclosed and no Colorado-specific federal advisory has appeared. Reporting has not consistently identified which devices were reached, so we are not naming a device type. What matters for operators is the pattern. Silenced alarms, lost remote view and changed pump behaviour are the same effects documented in the summer campaign against internet-facing controllers (see the water campaign card), and they have landed again on the kind of system that campaign has favoured: very small, with few or no dedicated IT staff. - Colorado Governor’s office statement, reported by Reuters, AP, Axios Denver, the Denver Post and KRDO - Intrusions late Aug 2026; confirmed by the Governor’s office 18 Sep 2026; follow-on reporting through 22 Sep 2026, re-checked 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Six weeks on, the water campaign has not stopped — and the documented impact is still lost view, altered logic and disabled alarms
item.category: Incident — Multi-state campaign against water utilities
item.description: Reporting on 5 September indicates Iranian government-linked operators have continued probing internet-exposed control systems at water utilities, telecommunications providers and energy companies in recent weeks, without so far producing damage on the scale of the July wave. That is the current status of a campaign whose documented effects remain the reason to care: the underlying FBI alert describes actors reaching internet-facing Rockwell MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers, modifying or deleting project-file logic, manipulating what HMI and SCADA screens displayed, and disabling shutdown and alarm blocks — unsafe conditions with normal-looking readings. Consequences reported at affected utilities include loss of view, pressure loss and flooding. Utilities in at least a dozen states have reported possible intrusions since 27 July; more than 30 Minnesota community systems were hit on 26–27 July. - FBI cyber alert on water and wastewater sector PLC targeting — continued-targeting update reported by NBC News, 5 Sep 2026 - Continued-targeting reporting 5 Sep 2026; FBI alert published August 2026 covering activity from 27 Jul 2026; Minnesota action 26–27 Jul 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A Bavarian utility lost its IT systems to ransomware — water kept flowing, but customer bank details may be exposed
item.category: Incident — Ransomware at a German utility supplying electricity and water
item.description: Stadtwerke Landsberg in Bavaria says attackers encrypted its central IT systems overnight into 1 September in what it calls a targeted criminal cyberattack. The utility’s own press releases confirm the incident and a rebuild under way, and The Record, citing the utility, reports that electricity, water and other essential services kept running; the visible disruption was limited phone and email contact. On 7 September the utility posted a GDPR data-subject notification saying it cannot rule out access to or theft of customer data, including names, addresses, contact details and bank details. No ransomware group has claimed the attack and no extortion demand is known. This is an IT-side incident with no reported operational impact, and it belongs here for that reason: IT was lost while supply continued, which is exactly the outcome separation between business and control systems is meant to buy. Whether it would hold at your utility is worth testing before an incident answers the question. - Stadtwerke Landsberg press releases and GDPR notice, reported by The Record - Attack 1 Sep 2026; GDPR notice posted 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Infostealer malware has captured logins from nearly one in five US water and wastewater organisations SpyCloud checked — 258 of them for OT or remote access
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Credential exposure, not intrusion
item.description: SpyCloud has published research analysing about 10,000 EPA-registered water and wastewater organisations and their vendors against its infostealer data. It found 1,787 organisations with active infostealer exposure, and 258 whose exposed credentials were for OT or remote-access systems. In one supply-chain example, a single infected device at an advanced-metering technology provider held saved logins for roughly 167 individual utility metering portals. TechCrunch and CyberScoop reported the findings on 22 September. SpyCloud is explicit about the limits: the data measures identity exposure, not confirmed intrusion, and does not prove any water utility has been breached. Exposure was concentrated in larger operators and the vendor supply chain, and small utilities were largely underrepresented. TechCrunch adds that SpyCloud found no evidence the Iran-linked water intrusions relied on stolen passwords. No utilities or vendors are named. The point for operators is a second route in alongside exposed controllers: a password stolen from a contractor’s or vendor’s home laptop works on your remote-access portal unless something else is also required. - SpyCloud research on water-sector identity exposure, reported by TechCrunch and CyberScoop - SpyCloud research dated 20 Sep 2026; TechCrunch and CyberScoop reporting 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s new detection guidance starts from the assumption that the attacker gets in — then makes them trip over something
item.category: Guidance — CISA detection guidance for critical infrastructure
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. It defines decoys as assets that look like legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence or collect intelligence on them, and it recommends tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens alongside Zero Trust on the explicit assumption that an attacker will eventually obtain some network access. The guide organises planning around the three MITRE Engage goals — expose, affect, elicit — and maps the resulting detections to ATT&CK, with particular attention to the living-off-the-land activity that conventional tooling misses. It sets out three phases, preparation, execution and analysis, and advises iterating continuously with red-team exercises. For water and wastewater the appeal is the economics rather than the novelty: a decoy account, a fake historian export or a bogus engineering-workstation credential costs nothing to run, changes nothing about production systems, and produces an alert that is almost never a false positive — which is a very different proposition from adding monitoring to a plant network that cannot be taken down. We have seen a secondhand report that the guide contains a water-sector case study; the CISA document itself could not be retrieved to confirm that, so it is not asserted here. - CISA, “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reporting via SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber; the CISA PDF was not retrievable at compile time - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A China-linked crew is emptying self-hosted code servers — and one of the hauls was SCADA and HMI source code
item.category: Threat intel — Code repositories at industrial suppliers
item.description: Acronis researchers describe a campaign they attribute, with moderate confidence, to a China-nexus actor they call Red Heron, exploiting a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code-repository platform (CVE-2026-60004) since 29 July 2026. Acronis, the primary source, counts 11 compromised targets in five countries: Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the US and Sri Lanka. Secondary reports give other tallies. Two victims should concern industrial operators directly: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-monitoring products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm that lost infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens. Acronis documents a new Linux LD_PRELOAD rootkit, SIXZUT. The Hacker News also reports a custom implant, JITTERLY, with more than thirty commands. For a water utility the exposure is second-hand but real, because the repository at risk is almost never yours — it is your integrator’s. Ladder logic, HMI projects, network diagrams, VPN configurations and device passwords for dozens of small systems routinely sit in one self-hosted Git server that nobody involved treats as critical infrastructure. - Acronis TRU research of 13 Sep 2026, reported by The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber - Reported 14–15 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from 29 Jul 2026 onward

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge, with utility-sector victims doubling month on month from five to ten — the sharpest sectoral increase in the set. One of those named is a water company: Alto Calore Servizi, which supplies the Avellino province of southern Italy, listed by the Titan group. That is a leak-site claim rather than a confirmation by the utility, and nothing published indicates treatment or distribution control was touched. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Utilities feature prominently in the monthly breakdown, and for water systems the pattern is familiar: encryption on the corporate side, with the operational cost showing up in billing, SCADA historian access, work orders and the ability to reach an integrator for support. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For a water utility with two operators and no security budget, this is the most useful framing available: you may not be able to keep an attacker out of a network, but you can design the plant so that a compromise cannot produce an unsafe dose or an overflow. Mechanical limits and analogue interlocks are cybersecurity controls. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Exposed PLCs and flat remote access at small US water utilities draw fresh vendor attention
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector exposure
item.description: Reporting on 15 September covered a vendor push specifically aimed at the exposed-PLC and remote-access problem facing small US water and electric utilities — the gap that has driven federal warnings all summer. This is the exposure the FBI and EPA described in their 30 July public service announcement, restated as a market problem: the utilities most likely to have a PLC on the public internet are the ones least able to do anything about it. The underlying facts are the ones that matter and they are already federally documented: the FBI and EPA warned on 30 July that actors were reaching internet-facing Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs at water and wastewater utilities, changing IP addresses and passwords, and causing loss of view and in some cases loss of control, with reported effects including pressure loss and flooding. A subsequent internet-wide scan reported by CyberScoop found roughly 4,400 exposed programmable logic controllers still reachable, including 22 in cities that had recently been attacked. Vendor marketing aside, the exposure is real, measured and unresolved. - FBI and EPA public service announcement of 30 July 2026, CyberScoop exposure scan reporting, and vendor coverage via Industrial Cyber - FBI/EPA PSA 30 Jul 2026; vendor coverage 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Four exploited edge and management flaws went into KEV on 22 September with a three-day deadline — including the SD-WAN orchestrator that configures remote sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed edge and management plane
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September, with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. For water utilities the one to chase first is CVE-2026-93952 in Arista’s on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVSS v3.1 10.0), an input-validation flaw that Arista’s Security Advisory 0183 says is known to be actively exploited. It is reachable only where certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication is configured, and Arista’s hosted orchestrators are already patched. An SD-WAN orchestrator pushes configuration to every edge it manages, which at a utility can mean the links to pump stations, lift stations and remote tanks. The second is CVE-2026-94127 in F5 BIG-IP APM (CVSS 9.8), a heap overflow giving unauthenticated code execution, exposed only where APM acts as an OAuth authorization server (F5 K000162605). The third is CVE-2026-93616 in Check Point’s Security Management Server (CVSS 9.8), a pre-authentication path traversal that Check Point says was used in a handful of targeted attacks on 23 July, two months before its 22 September fix. It is a different flaw from CVE-2026-91843 (see the Check Point management card). The fourth, Check Point’s VPN flaw CVE-2026-85102, has its own card. No attribution has been published for any of them, and no water utility has been named as a victim. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities addition of 22 Sep 2026; Arista Security Advisory 0183, F5 K000162605 and Check Point’s 22 Sep advisory, corroborated by SecurityAffairs, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and BleepingComputer - Added to KEV 22 Sep 2026; federal due date 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A CVSS 9.8 flaw in lwIP’s MQTT client could sit deep inside embedded field gear — and nobody yet knows which water devices ship it
item.category: Critical Advisory — Embedded TCP/IP stack, supply chain
item.description: CISA published two advisories on 22 September for lwIP, the open-source lightweight TCP/IP stack embedded in a wide range of microcontroller-based devices. ICSA-26-265-01 covers CVE-2026-87121 in lwIP’s MQTT client application, an out-of-bounds write rated CVSS 9.8 (network-reachable, no authentication, no user interaction) that may allow an attacker to gain full code execution on the device. ICSA-26-265-02 is a second lwIP advisory published the same day. Neither is reported as exploited and neither is in KEV. The difficulty for utilities is that lwIP is a component, not a product: device makers compile it into their firmware, and only devices that include and use the MQTT client are exposed to CVE-2026-87121. MQTT is widely used for telemetry and IIoT gateways — the kind of equipment small systems use for remote tank and pump-station monitoring. At compile time no downstream vendor had published product-by-product impact, and Ubuntu lists its own lwip package as still under evaluation. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-265-01 and ICSA-26-265-02; CVE record via the Ubuntu security tracker - Published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A small-office managed switch goes into KEV after nearly a thousand were quietly stripped of their configurations and root password hashes — the class of switch that ends up in a pump-house cabinet
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, small-site network switch
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel fixed it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the equivalent build for each model; Zyxel’s advisory gives no CVSS and we do not invent one. The KEV listing says LAN-based, which means the exposure is management-plane reachability rather than a raw internet-facing service. What made it exploited is described in a GreyNoise report published the same day: a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed by GreyNoise as a Chinese speaker, exploited 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries, 129 of them in the United States, using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP. GreyNoise counts 564 of the victims as running factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws in July and has probed Gitea (CVE-2026-60004, the flaw in the Red Heron card), UniFi, Proxmox and PAN-OS GlobalProtect among others; GreyNoise infers overlap with Red Heron from shared command-and-control, which is an inference rather than an observation. The water relevance is editorial: the GS1900 is the low-cost managed switch an integrator specifies for a small plant, a booster station or a well house, and a stolen configuration from one of them contains VLAN layout, SNMP strings and the credential hashes an attacker needs to move from the office network to the controls. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (added 21 Sep 2026), GreyNoise research of 21 Sep 2026 and Zyxel security advisory of 16 Jun 2026 - KEV listing 21 Sep 2026; GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; Zyxel fix 16 Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Rockwell revises its PLC lockout-recovery notice for the fifth time — Micro820 and Micro850 now join the MicroLogix controllers that attackers were setting passwords on
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, small-site PLCs
item.description: On 18 September Rockwell Automation issued revision 5.0 of SD1790, the notice titled “Important Hardening Guidance … and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown” that it first published on 30 July. The revision extends the recovery and hardening instructions to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 it already covered. The notice references the FBI public service announcement of 30 July, which described attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none had existed, so that operators were locked out of their own controllers. There is no CVE; the guidance is to remove controllers from internet exposure, put remote access behind a VPN, isolate with a firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 contains no new incident data; the exploitation is the premise of the document rather than a new finding, and Rockwell has published no new security advisories between 10 and 24 September (its last batch was 1 September). The water relevance needs no editorial stretch: MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 are the controllers named in the FBI water-sector alert behind the campaign card, and the Micro800 family is what a small utility buys to replace them. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790, revision 5.0 - Revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026; original notice 30 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Three Linux kernel flaws went into KEV with a three-day deadline that has now passed — and the kernel sits under more of a treatment plant than most inventories show
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, operating-system layer
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September that has now passed: CVE-2025-39964, a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto interface; CVE-2026-53266, an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling; and CVE-2025-39682, a flaw in kTLS zero-length record handling. All three are local flaws, which is to say they matter to an attacker who already has a foothold on the machine and wants root. No source we found attributes the exploitation to any actor, and CISA’s catalog entries do not describe it. We print no CVSS scores because published figures differ from source to source; take the vendor score for your distribution. Note that cisa.gov could not be retrieved when this edition was compiled, so the listings were confirmed through several secondary reports of the two CISA alerts. These are not the same flaw as the “Copy Fail” kernel bug CVE-2026-31431 in the ABB Edgenius advisory of 17 September. The water relevance is editorial and structural: Linux is the operating system inside HMI panels, edge gateways, industrial firewalls, cellular routers and the historian or jump host in the OT DMZ, and a kernel privilege-escalation flaw is what turns the foothold gained through an exploited edge appliance into control of the box that reaches the plant. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, two alerts of 18 Sep 2026 — confirmed via multiple secondary reports; cisa.gov was not retrievable at compile time - KEV listings added 18 Sep 2026; federal deadline 21 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Twenty-two flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two of them CVSS 9.8 — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
item.category: Advisory — CERT@VDE, IO-Link master modules, vulnerability research
item.description: CERT@VDE published advisory VDE-2026-014 on 16 September covering 22 vulnerabilities in the firmware of Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers Gabriele Quagliarella and Luca Borzacchiello. Firmware before 1.7.4 is affected and the fix is 1.7.8. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. The remainder, CVE-2026-27547 through -27564, are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorization flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. The same firmware is sold rebadged, so the advisory comes in three parts: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs, same fix version, same day) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters (VDE-2026-028). No exploitation is reported and no CISA advisory had appeared by 24 September. The water relevance is editorial: IO-Link masters are the box between the PLC and the level, pressure, flow and valve-position sensors on a packaged treatment skid or dosing system, and a master that runs attacker-supplied shell scripts can feed the controller whatever readings it likes. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-014, VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; Nozomi Networks Labs research - Published 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] One malformed login request can take a Moxa TN-4500B switch down — no credentials needed, fixed in firmware 2.1
item.category: Advisory — Vendor PSIRT, ruggedised industrial Ethernet switch
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in the TN-4500B series of ruggedised Ethernet switches, firmware 2.0 and earlier. It is an unauthenticated out-of-bounds write in the way the web login handles the username field, and the result is a denial of service; Moxa scores it CVSS v4 8.8 with high availability impact and no confidentiality impact. The fix is firmware 2.1, and no exploitation has been reported. The TN-4500B is built to the EN 50155 rolling-stock standard and is more common on trains and trackside than in a treatment plant, where Moxa’s EDS line dominates, so this is not a sector-listed advisory and the inclusion is editorial. It is here for two reasons: some utilities standardise on the TN line for harsh remote sites, and an unauthenticated fault in a switch’s web login that knocks the switch offline is the same class of flaw that keeps appearing across industrial switches from every vendor, so the mitigation — nothing can reach the management page except a management network — is worth applying regardless of the model on the shelf. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 - Published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] One crafted network message can stop ABB Freelance DCS controllers — the fix is already in rollups many sites never installed
item.category: Advisory — Vendor PSIRT, process DCS controllers
item.description: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a flaw reserved in 2023 and disclosed only now. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the controller on the network can send a specially crafted message that makes it stop. ABB’s CSAF record scores it CVSS v3.1 7.5 (availability impact only). Affected are the Freelance AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers and the DCP controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier through 2019 SP1. The fixes already ship in existing update rollups: 2013 SP1 RU06 or later, 2016 SP1 RU07 or later, 2019 SP1 RU03 or later and 2019 SP1 FP1. Freelance 2024 is not affected. ABB says it had no reports of exploitation and no prior public disclosure when it issued the advisory. The water relevance is an editorial judgement rather than a vendor sector list: Freelance is a process DCS found in treatment plants, and many installations run long-lived releases that never received the later rollups. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 7PAA010706 (CSAF) - Published 18 Sep 2026; CVE reserved 2023

item.title: [Critical] The policy engine that decides who gets onto the plant network has a CVSS 10 bypass, exploited as a zero-day
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September covering CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC scored CVSS 10.0. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker reach the web-based management interface. Cisco states plainly that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, 16 September, with a three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds; ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and gets no fix, so those deployments need migrating. Singapore’s CSA issued its own alert on 21 September urging patching. Neither Cisco nor CISA has published attribution, and no critical-infrastructure or OT targeting has been claimed — the water relevance here is editorial rather than reported: where a utility or its county IT department uses ISE for 802.1X and network access control, it is often the component that decides which devices and which contractor laptops land on the plant VLAN rather than the business one. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published and KEV listing added 16 Sep 2026; federal deadline 19 Sep 2026 passed; CSA Singapore alert 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A crafted email is enough to get root on a Cisco email gateway — exploited, and in KEV since 14 September
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX, first published 14 September, describes CVE-2026-76461: a SQL injection flaw in AsyncOS email parsing on Cisco Secure Email Gateway, scored CVSS 9.8. An unauthenticated attacker who simply sends a specially crafted message containing malicious SQL can reach arbitrary SQL and command execution with root privileges, with no user interaction required. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026, and CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 14 September with a federal remediation deadline of 17 September, now passed. Both physical and virtual appliances are affected regardless of configuration, and Shadowserver counted more than 400 exposed appliances. Fixed builds start at 16.5.0-780, with separate fixes for the 16.0 and 15.5 lines; outlets disagree on the exact build strings, so take them from the Cisco advisory. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed, though researchers have noted the flaw would suit state-linked espionage. For a utility this is an enterprise-side exposure rather than a control-system one, and that is precisely how the last two years of OT incidents began: on-premises gateways carry more pivot risk than hosted ones because they sit inside the network that reaches the historian and the engineering workstations. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — corroborated by BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Cybersecurity Dive - Advisory published and KEV listing added 14 Sep 2026; reporting through 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 17 September batch is seven new advisories plus one update — and the Modicon M340 fix is the one most water plants need
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS batch, ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 plus ICSA-26-211-07 Update A
item.description: CISA’s bulletin for Thursday 17 September lists eight items: seven new ICS advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update. The new advisories cover Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (models 750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The highest score we can verify in the batch is CVE-2026-15688 in GX Works3, an authentication-algorithm flaw affecting all versions, rated CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues (CVE-2026-86520 at 7.5, CVE-2026-86689 at 5.9 and CVE-2026-77960 at 5.3) fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA’s CSAF records now cover the Schneider and ABB advisories. ICSA-26-260-04 is CVE-2025-6625 in Modicon M340 and its Ethernet modules, a crafted-FTP-command denial of service rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 (v4 8.7), fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70; it republishes a Schneider advisory first issued in August 2025 (the CVE year is 2025, not 2026), and CISA lists Water and Wastewater among its sectors. ICSA-26-260-05 covers NetBotz 5 CVE-2026-13336 (v3.1 6.4, v4 7.3) and CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0; Schneider originally published the NetBotz and PowerChute advisories on 11 August, and ABB the Edgenius one on 25 June, so CISA is republishing rather than breaking these. ICSA-26-260-06 is the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 (7.8) in ABB Ability Edgenius, fixed in 3.2.4.1. ICSA-26-260-07 is CVE-2026-13348 in PowerChute Serial Shutdown (v3.1 5.3, v4 6.9), fixed in v1.6. The Mitsubishi and Hitachi Energy records had still not reached the mirror, so we print no further detail for Hitachi. CISA reports no exploitation for any advisory in the batch. The eighth item, ICSA-26-211-07 Update A on the Mitsubishi Electric CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol, was revised on 17 September to add eight newly affected products and remove three. CISA published a further batch on 22 September; its most broadly relevant items for water are the lwIP advisories (see the lwIP card). The water relevance is an editorial judgement rather than a CISA sector assignment: Modicon M340 is a widely deployed process controller and NetBotz 5 is cabinet environmental monitoring, both of which turn up in treatment plants and pump stations. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 (advisory titles confirmed; CVE and CVSS detail taken from CISA’s public CSAF records, which cover -01 and -04 to -07; -02 and -03 not yet in the mirror) - Published 17 Sep 2026; ICSA-26-211-07 Update A 17 Sep 2026; re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 9.8 flaw in mySCADA myPRO Manager could hand an attacker the management functions — and the SMS modem behind them
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA management software, CISA ICSA-26-258-03
item.description: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. CVE-2026-73807 is a missing-authorization flaw scored CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, scored 6.3, is missing authentication for a critical function. Together they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. CISA lists water and wastewater among the affected sectors, alongside energy, critical manufacturing, food and agriculture, and transportation. The fix is version 2.2, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. For a utility the SMS path deserves as much attention as the console: if on-call alarm texts go out through that modem, messages an attacker can send through it could muddy the alarms operators rely on at night. CISA’s machine-readable record for this advisory batch was posted to its public CSAF repository on 15 September and was still awaiting merge when this edition was compiled. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 (CSAF record in CISA’s public repository, pending merge at compile time) - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and water and wastewater teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Small and mid-size water utilities increasingly keep SCADA integration scripts, HMI project exports, historian queries and vendor credentials in a self-hosted GitLab that the OT team stood up years ago and nobody patches. An unauthenticated file read against it yields exactly the material an attacker needs to understand dosing, pumping and lift-station logic before touching a single PLC. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to 12 flaws, several of them chainable to root on an OT edge device
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September. Across the whole body of work the count is twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, with CVSS scores spanning 5.3 to 8.5. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client versions through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory and fixes from V4.0 HF0 onward. The finding that matters is not any single score: Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onward. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two corrections to how this story has been framed, including in our own previous edition. The four PROFINET DCP memory-corruption flaws (CVE-2025-40575 to CVE-2025-40578, each CVSS 5.3 and denial-of-service only) came from the first part of the research, published 10 September, and those CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18. What happened on 15 September was an update to that existing advisory, adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes — not a new critical advisory. Note too that the CVE identifiers for this research line carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 disclosure dates, so match them against Siemens’ own security advisory before acting on an identifier. - Nozomi Networks Labs research (parts one and two) and Siemens ProductCERT, with CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 — reporting via Industrial Cyber; the Nozomi blog was not retrieved directly for this edition - Second research publication 18 Sep 2026; first part 10 Sep 2026; CISA advisory updated 15 Sep 2026; CVEs originally disclosed May 2025

item.title: [Medium] Schneider’s SCADAPack x70 RTUs protect stored credentials too weakly — and these are the boxes at your well fields and lift stations
item.category: Advisory — RTUs at water and wastewater remote sites
item.description: Alongside the Modicon M580 authentication flaw in the same 8 September round, Schneider Electric issued advisory SEVD-2026-251-03 covering insufficiently protected credentials in the SCADAPack x70 family — the 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x remote terminal units. Schneider rates it medium and on its own terms that is fair: an attacker has to reach the device or the traffic to it before the weakness is worth anything. The reason it belongs on a water dashboard is what that access buys in a sector where one credential is usually the whole fleet’s credential. SCADAPack RTUs are the standard workhorse at unstaffed remote sites — well fields, lift stations, booster stations, tank and reservoir telemetry — and they are also among the devices most likely to sit behind a cellular modem with a public address. Set that against the documented technique of the July campaign, where actors who reached internet-facing controllers changed passwords and IP addresses to lock operators out, and a credential recoverable from one roadside cabinet stops reading like a medium-severity abstraction. CISA republished the advisory on 15 September as ICSA-26-258-04, scoring the flaw CVSS v3 6.5, reporting no known public exploitation, and recommending role-based access control, network segmentation and the RTU’s own firewall service as mitigations. - Schneider Electric security notification SEVD-2026-251-03, republished by CISA as ICSA-26-258-04 - Published 8 Sep 2026; CISA republication 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Schneider patches a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580, the controller running plenty of treatment plants
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday, Schneider Electric
item.description: Schneider Electric published four security advisories on 8 September, and the one water and wastewater operators need to read first covers Modicon M580 and Modicon M580 Safety controllers. CVE-2026-3869, scored CVSS 9.2, is a critical authentication vulnerability in the controller itself. M580 is not niche equipment in this sector: it runs filtration trains, chemical dosing skids, pump stations and lift stations across utilities of every size, and the Safety variant is deployed precisely where a failure has consequences beyond lost production. Schneider reports no exploitation. Alongside it the company fixed a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, the RTU formerly sold as Easergy T300 and widely used for remote site telemetry, plus EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert and a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 — the RTU family many systems run for lift-station, remote-well and booster-station telemetry, which makes it the most water-specific item in the batch even at a lower score. The secondary reporting on the SCADAPack x70 issue carried no CVE identifier and no CVSS vector, only the vendor’s medium rating, so confirm the reference against Schneider Electric’s own security notification before you log it against an asset. For most utilities that is three of four advisories touching equipment already in the ground. - Schneider Electric security advisories of 8 Sep 2026 — summarised in SecurityWeek’s September ICS Patch Tuesday round-up - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The MikroTik router chain moves from theory to practice — CERT Polska confirms real attacks
item.category: Critical Advisory — Now confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS flaws known as the “MikroTrick” chain, disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited, are now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass at CVSS 9.2, with CVE-2026-86060, an SSH privilege-escalation flaw also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. The reason it belongs on a water dashboard is placement rather than any confirmed water victim: inexpensive routers of this class turn up at remote pump and lift stations, on cellular backhaul links and inside integrator-supplied remote-access kit, and those are the devices least likely to appear in an asset register or a patch cycle. - CERT Polska alert of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber - Exploitation confirmed 9 Sep 2026; activity observed from about 2 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 12 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Check Point confirms attacks on its CVSS 9.8 VPN flaw since 12 September — now in KEV, with fixes out since 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Check Point said in a 22 September advisory that it has observed a wave of exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-85102 on Spark firewalls starting 12 September, three days after it released fixes on 9 September. The flaw, rated CVSS 9.8, is improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation and gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on Security Gateways and Spark appliances. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal due date of 25 September. Check Point has not given a victim count or attribution, but it has published indicators: exploitation certificates with the subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. The Dutch NCSC had warned on 12 September that exploitation of this flaw and its companion, CVE-2026-85103, was imminent; only CVE-2026-85102 is reported as exploited. A separate Check Point management-server flaw went into KEV the same day (see the 22 September KEV card). It belongs on a water dashboard because of what sits behind that gateway at a utility of any size: the SCADA integrator’s support tunnel, the instrumentation vendor’s remote diagnostics, and the operator VPN that staff use to check the plant at 2 am from home. Spark is Check Point’s small-business firewall line — the kind of appliance small systems and their contractors run. - Check Point security advisory of 22 Sep 2026 and CISA KEV; earlier Dutch NCSC warning reported by BleepingComputer - Fixes released 9 Sep 2026; exploitation from 12 Sep 2026; added to KEV 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A second Check Point flaw, this time in the server that writes the firewall policy — CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated root, not exploited
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management server, unauthenticated RCE
item.description: Check Point has patched CVE-2026-91843, rated CVSS 9.8, in its Security Management Server and Log Server, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and SecurityWeek on 18 September. It is a stack overflow in the login process: an unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can give a remote attacker code execution as root. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be confirmed in the vendor text, so check your own configuration rather than relying on it. Affected, per the reporting on advisory sk1000155: R82.10 up to Jumbo Hotfix Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, all R82.20 builds, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines. Multi-Domain Server is affected; Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. Check Point says there is no indication of exploitation in the wild. This is separate from the two VPN flaws the Dutch NCSC warned about on 12 September. It is also separate from CVE-2026-93616, a different management-server flaw that Check Point says was exploited in targeted attacks in July and that CISA added to KEV on 22 September (see the 22 September KEV card); CVE-2026-91843 itself remains unexploited. For a utility the concern is position, not score: the management server is where the rules between the business network and the treatment plant are written, so whoever owns it can loosen them. - Check Point advisory sk1000155, as reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek — vendor page not directly accessible at compile time - Reported 17 Sep 2026; SecurityWeek round-up 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Five more exploited flaws go into KEV — including the remote-support tool your SCADA integrator logs in with
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September after evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors, while ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly allowed unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain covered separately here. For a water or wastewater utility the ScreenConnect item is the one that lands closest to home: remote-support software is how most integrators and instrumentation vendors reach an HMI or engineering workstation, it is often installed during commissioning and never reviewed, and it frequently runs with local administrator rights on the one machine that can program the PLCs. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The firewall console that keeps your business network out of SCADA is being exploited — by a cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm’s, and by one Talos assesses as a Qilin ransomware affiliate
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited firewall-management flaw, in KEV
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active attack. The CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker send crafted HTTP requests and take root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV on 9 September with a federal deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three clusters exploiting FMC: UAT-12197, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and deliver a malicious JAR file; UAT-11823, whose tooling Talos says overlaps with the Russian APT Sandworm (an overlap, not an attribution) and which delivered Cyclops Blink malware; and UAT-11988, whose tactics Talos assesses as consistent with Qilin ransomware affiliates, which used an earlier FMC static-credential flaw, CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3, not in KEV), to get in, steal credentials and build a list of endpoints to target for encryption. Deployment of ransomware through FMC has not been reported. On 16 September Cisco shipped a separate hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN). It fixes eight internally found flaws, CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, with a maximum CVSS of 9.9, and accompanies the exploited FMC flaws, so plan it into the same maintenance window. For a water utility the relevance is direct. After July’s PLC campaign the advice to the sector was to get controllers off the internet and put a properly configured firewall between business systems and treatment control. FMC is where that firewall is configured, and root on FMC means an attacker can quietly rewrite the rules you are relying on. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening release 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Siemens issues nine advisories in the same round, and the management layer is where water utilities are exposed
item.category: Critical Advisory — September ICS Patch Tuesday, Siemens and Aveva
item.description: Alongside the Schneider Electric fixes covered above, Siemens published nine advisories on 8 September, seven of them on the day. The headline item is a CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay family, which reaches only the larger water utilities that own high-voltage supply or substation assets. The rest of the batch is closer to home for most systems: critical findings in Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT — the platform and remote-management tier that sits above process equipment rather than in it — plus the start of a fix roll-out for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8 across affected product lines. Aveva separately disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA formalised them on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: CVE-2026-81821, a hardcoded cryptographic key, and CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing, both CVSS 8.4, alongside a missing-authorisation flaw at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, all fixed in the Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2 security update. The advisory is aimed at pipeline operators, but it is worth noting for utilities running long raw-water or transmission mains on that platform. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and the wider Siemens and Aveva advisories of 8 Sep 2026, plus CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 on Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor — summarised by SecurityWeek and ISSSource - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026 (SSA-142885 v1.0); CISA ICSA-26-253-01 published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] NIST’s rewrite of the core OT security guide now names water and wastewater systems in scope — comments close 30 November
item.category: Policy — Federal OT security guidance
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November 2026. The revision expands the scope beyond traditional industrial control systems to cover building automation and control systems, water and wastewater systems, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. It is restructured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management reorganised under the CSF Govern function; it adds architecture guidance on applying zero-trust principles to protect system management functions; and it expands guidance on OT security controls, including asset management and network monitoring and detection. Industrial Cyber’s 22 September write-up notes the draft describes a mature OT defence mindset as consequence-driven. SP 800-82 is a common reference in OT assessments, so the water material is worth reading while it can still be changed. - NIST Computer Security Resource Center, SP 800-82 Rev. 4 initial public draft; reported by Industrial Cyber - Draft released 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s Cyber Storm X rehearsed a nation-state attack on water and wastewater — and the lessons are due to be published
item.category: Policy — National cyber exercise
item.description: CISA said on 22 September that it had run Cyber Storm X, the latest in its national cyber exercise series, over four days with about 2,000 participants from more than 200 organisations across government and the private sector. The scenario was a nation-state adversary targeting transportation, including rail and ports, and the water and wastewater sector. Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said exercises make sure “our plans, policies, and partnerships are ready when we need them.” CISA says it will work with participating organisations to compile a public after-action report with observations, analyses and recommendations. The exercise dates were not given in the reporting. An exercise report is not a control, but it is one of the few places the federal view of how a water-sector crisis would be coordinated gets written down. - CISA news release, reported by Industrial Cyber (CISA page not directly accessible at compile time) - Announced 22 Sep 2026; after-action report to follow

item.title: [Info] CISA is retiring the weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether anyone at your utility reads it
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA publication change
item.description: CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September, pointing readers instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, its alerts and its advisories. The agency frames the change as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in Binding Operational Directive 26-04 in June 2026: a weekly list of everything published is a poor substitute for a shorter list of what is actually being exploited. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected — the ICS-CERT advisory stream and the KEV catalog both continue. The practical question for a water utility is whether that weekly digest was somebody’s routine. In systems with no dedicated security staff it is often the one recurring email that prompts a look at patching at all, and when it stops arriving on 28 September nothing will replace it automatically. Reported here factually as a change to a public data source. - CISA announcement of the Vulnerability Summary bulletin retirement — reporting via SecurityWeek; the CISA page was not retrievable at compile time - Reported 17 Sep 2026; effective 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Low] States report they lack the money and staff to defend water and energy systems
item.category: Policy — State capacity to defend water and energy infrastructure
item.description: A report from NASCIO and GDIT released on 11 September finds that state and local governments do not have the funding or staff to protect water, energy and other critical sectors, and cites the July 2026 Iran-linked water system campaign as context. Its recommendations are to inventory high-risk critical infrastructure, set baseline hygiene standards, require incident reporting, and expand shared services for local entities. It is a policy document rather than threat intelligence, but it matters to a small water system for a practical reason: the state programmes many utilities expect to lean on are saying they are stretched too. - NASCIO and GDIT report, reported by Cybersecurity Dive - Published 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Water utilities are not the regulated party here — the makers of the PLCs, HMIs, dosing controllers and cellular gateways they buy are. The practical effect is that vulnerability information about that equipment should start arriving faster and through a single channel. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting is live — your pump and dosing vendors now have 24 hours to report an exploited flaw
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now report an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident to ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with detail on the exploit and mitigation status, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available. They must also notify affected users. The obligations reach any manufacturer placing products on the EU market, wherever it is based, with penalties up to €15 million. For a US water utility this is not a compliance obligation — it is a supply-side change. PLC, HMI, SCADA, chlorine-analyser and pump-controller vendors selling into Europe are now on a 24-hour clock, so exploitation-confirmed disclosures about the equipment in your plant should arrive sooner and in a more consistent shape. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — a problem sharpest at utilities with one person on call
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The argument is operational rather than ideological: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull people away from containment in the hours when containment still helps. Water and wastewater utilities feel this more acutely than most sectors, not because their obligations are heavier but because the same person is often the operator, the incident commander and the one filing to the state primacy agency, WaterISAC, the EPA and, potentially, CISA. At a system serving a few thousand people that is not a coordination problem, it is a single point of failure. The analysis arrives as CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO data, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Medium] A federal-state pilot puts free vulnerability hunting into 250 Texas water systems — and it is meant to scale
item.category: Policy — Federal/state water cybersecurity pilot
item.description: Texas Governor Greg Abbott and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross announced Project Watershed 250 on 31 August in San Antonio: a six-month pilot using Texas as a testing ground to find and help fix vulnerabilities across participating water systems, with EPA and CISA as federal partners and Texas Cyber Command alongside them. Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, Reflection AI and Dragos are taking part; utilities pay nothing. Officials say the programme was already in development before the July intrusions that hit community water systems in Minnesota and other states, and that the intent is to expand the model nationally. For a small utility the significant word is “free” — the cost of an assessment has been the standing excuse for not having one. - Office of the National Cyber Director and Texas Governor’s office announcement — reported by Nextgov/FCW, Route Fifty and Infosecurity Magazine - Announced 31 Aug 2026; six-month pilot period
